danish.title: Niende bog (1812) — Kapitel 5
paragraphs: Davout var for Napoleon, hvad Araktjejev var for Aleksandr — selv om han ikke var en kujon som Araktjejev, var han lige så nøjagtig, lige så grusom og lige så ude af stand til at udtrykke sin hengivenhed for sin hersker på anden vis end ved grusomhed.

I staternes organisme er sådanne mennesker nødvendige, ligesom ulve er nødvendige i naturens organisme, og de findes altid, træder altid frem og hævder sig, hvor upassende deres tilstedeværelse og nærhed til statsoverhovedet end måtte forekomme. Denne uafvendelighed alene kan forklare, hvordan den grusomme Araktjejev, der med egne hænder rev overskægget af en grenader, hvis svage nerver gjorde ham ude af stand til at se fare i øjnene, og som hverken var en dannet mand eller en hofmand, formåede at bevare sin magtfulde position hos Aleksandr, hvis egen karakter var ridderlig, ædel og mild.

Balasjov fandt Davout siddende på en tønde i skuret ved en bondehytte og skrive — han reviderede regnskaber. Han kunne have fået bedre kvarterer, men marskal Davout var en af de mennesker, der med vilje sætter sig i de mest nedslående omgivelser for at have en berettigelse for at være gnaven. Af samme grund er de altid travlt optaget og har altid hastværk. »Hvordan kan jeg tænke på livets lyse sider, når jeg som du ser sidder på en tønde og arbejder i et snavset skur?« syntes hans ansigtsudtryk at sige. Den største glæde og nødvendighed for sådanne mennesker, når de møder nogen der viser livlighed, er at fremvise deres egen triste, vedholdende travlhed. Davout undte sig denne glæde, da Balasjov blev ført ind. Han blev endnu mere fordybet i sit arbejde, da den russiske general trådte ind, og efter at have kigget hen over brillerne på Balasjovs ansigt, der var oplivet af morgenens skønhed og af samtalen med Murat, rejste han sig ikke og rørte sig ikke engang, men så endnu mere gnaven ud og smilede ondsindet.
Da han bemærkede det ubehagelige indtryk, denne modtagelse gjorde på Balasjovs ansigt, løftede Davout hovedet og spurgte koldt, hvad han ønskede.

Balasjov, der troede, at han kun kunne være modtaget på denne måde, fordi Davout ikke vidste, at han var generaladjudant hos kejser Aleksandr og endda hans udsending til Napoleon, skyndte sig at oplyse om sin rang og sit ærinde. Imod hans forventning blev Davout, efter at have hørt ham, endnu mere gnaven og grov.
»Hvor er Deres depeche?« spurgte han. »Giv mig den. Jeg sender den til kejseren.«
Balasjov svarede, at han havde fået ordre til at overrække den personligt til kejseren.
»Jeres kejsers ordrer adlydes i jeres hær, men her,« sagde Davout, »må I gøre, som man siger jer.«
Og som for at gøre den russiske general endnu mere bevidst om sin afhængighed af rå magt sendte Davout en adjudant for at hente vagthavende officer.
Balasjov tog pakken med kejserens brev frem og lagde den på bordet (der bestod af en dør med hængslerne stadig på, lagt hen over to tønder). Davout tog pakken og læste påskriften.
»De har fuld frihed til at behandle mig med respekt eller ej,« protesterede Balasjov, »men tillad mig at bemærke, at jeg har den ære at være generaladjudant hos Hans Majestæt...«
Davout så tavst på ham og nød tydeligvis de tegn på ophidselse og forvirring, der viste sig i Balasjovs ansigt.
»De vil blive behandlet, som det sig hør og bør,« sagde han, og idet han stak pakken i lommen, forlod han skuret.
Et minut senere kom marskalens adjudant, de Castrès, ind og førte Balasjov til de kvarterer, der var anvist ham.
Den dag spiste han middag med marskallen ved det samme bord på tønderne.

Næste dag red Davout tidligt ud og bad, da han havde kaldt Balasjov til sig, ham bydende om at blive, hvor han var, rykke med bagagetoget, hvis der kom ordre til det, og ikke tale med andre end monsieur de Castrès.

Efter fire dages ensomhed, kedsomhed og bevidsthed om sin afmagt og ubetydning — som var særlig stærk i modsætning til den magtsfære, han så kort forinden havde bevæget sig i — og efter flere marcher med marskalens bagage og den franske hær, der besatte hele egnen, blev Balasjov ført til Vilna, nu besat af franskmændene, gennem netop den port, han var redet ud af fire dage tidligere.
Næste dag kom den kejserlige kammerherre, grev de Turenne, til Balasjov og meddelte ham, at kejser Napoleon ønskede at beære ham med en audiens.

Fire dage forinden havde soldater fra Preobrasjénskregimentet stået vagt foran det hus, hvortil Balasjov nu blev ført, og nu stod der to franske grenaderer i blå uniformer, opknappede fortil, med lodne huer på hovedet, og en eskorte af husarer og uhlaner og et glimrende følge af adjudanter, pager og generaler, der ventede på, at Napoleon skulle komme ud, stod ved portalen, omkring hans sadelhest og hans mameluk, Rustan. Napoleon modtog Balasjov i netop det hus i Vilna, hvorfra Aleksandr havde sendt ham af sted på sit ærinde.

english.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: Davout was to Napoleon what Arakcheev was to Alexander — though not a coward like Arakcheev, he was equally precise, equally cruel, and equally unable to express his devotion to his sovereign except through cruelty.

In the organism of states such men are necessary, as wolves are necessary in the organism of nature, and they always exist, always appear and hold their ground, however incongruous their presence and proximity to the head of government may be. This inevitability alone can explain how the cruel Arakcheev, who tore out a grenadier's mustache with his own hands, whose weak nerves made him unable to face danger, and who was neither an educated man nor a courtier, was able to maintain his powerful position with Alexander, whose own character was chivalrous, noble, and gentle.

Balashev found Davout seated on a barrel in the shed of a peasant's hut, writing — he was auditing accounts. Better quarters could have been found for him, but Marshal Davout was one of those men who purposely put themselves in the most uncomfortable conditions to justify their being gloomy. For the same reason they are always hard at work and in a hurry. "How can I think about the bright side of life when, as you see, I'm sitting on a barrel and working in a dirty shed?" the expression on his face seemed to say. The chief pleasure and need of such men, when they encounter anyone who shows energy, is to display their own dreary, relentless activity. Davout indulged this pleasure when Balashev was brought in. He became still more absorbed in his work when the Russian general entered, and after glancing over his spectacles at Balashev's face — which was animated by the beauty of the morning and by his conversation with Murat — he did not rise or even stir, but scowled more deeply and sneered maliciously.
When he noticed the unpleasant impression this reception made on Balashev's face, Davout raised his head and coldly asked what he wanted.

Thinking he could only have been received this way because Davout didn't know that he was adjutant general to Emperor Alexander and even his envoy to Napoleon, Balashev hastened to state his rank and mission. Contrary to his expectation, Davout, after hearing him, became still surlier and ruder.
"Where is your dispatch?" he demanded. "Give it to me. I will send it to the Emperor."
Balashev replied that he had been ordered to hand it personally to the Emperor.
"Your Emperor's orders are obeyed in your army, but here," said Davout, "you must do as you're told."
And, as if to make the Russian general still more conscious of his helplessness before brute force, Davout sent an adjutant to call the officer on duty.

Balashev took out the packet containing the Emperor's letter and laid it on the table (made of a door with its hinges still attached, laid across two barrels). Davout took the packet and read the inscription.
"You are perfectly free to treat me with respect or not," protested Balashev, "but permit me to point out that I have the honor of being adjutant general to His Majesty..."
Davout glanced at him silently and clearly took pleasure in the signs of agitation and confusion on Balashev's face.
"You will be treated as is fitting," said he and, putting the packet in his pocket, left the shed.
A minute later the marshal's adjutant, de Castres, came in and took Balashev to the quarters assigned to him.
That day he dined with the marshal, at the same board on the barrels.

The next day Davout rode out early and, after calling for Balashev, bluntly ordered him to remain where he was, to move on with the baggage train if orders came for it to move, and to speak to no one except Monsieur de Castres.

After four days of solitude, boredom, and a painful sense of his own powerlessness and insignificance — particularly acute by contrast with the sphere of power in which he had so recently moved — and after several marches with the marshal's baggage and the French army, which occupied the whole district, Balashev was brought to Vilna — now occupied by the French — through the very gate by which he had left it four days earlier.
The next day the imperial gentleman-in-waiting, the Count de Turenne, came to Balashev and informed him of Emperor Napoleon's wish to honor him with an audience.

Four days before, sentinels of the Preobrazhensky regiment had stood in front of the house to which Balashev was conducted, and now two French grenadiers stood there in blue uniforms unbuttoned in front with shaggy caps on their heads, and an escort of hussars and Uhlans and a brilliant suite of aides-de-camp, pages, and generals, waiting for Napoleon to come out, were standing at the porch around his saddle horse and his Mameluke, Rustan. Napoleon received Balashev in the very house in Vilna from which Alexander had dispatched him on his mission.
